Product: Bumpons (small round clear dome head, DL24; also black flat-head and square variants)
Manufacturer: Sold by RNIB (Royal National Institute of Blind People, UK). Underlying manufacturer not verified (3M makes an industrial product called Bumpon, but RNIB's page does not say who makes these).
Target user: Blind and partially sighted people marking home or office equipment
Main functionality: Self-adhesive tactile bumps stuck onto controls to mark a position. RNIB lists washing machine settings, remote control buttons, oven settings, keyboard keys and door keys as uses.
Price: GBP 12.00 incl. VAT for a pack of 72 (the page also shows a GBP 10.00 variant, so the price is inconsistent). Source: https://shop.rnib.org.uk/products/small-round-clear-dome-head-bumpons
Installation requirements: Peel and stick. No tools or wiring. A sighted person or the user has to decide where each dot goes.
Accessibility features: Raised dome you can feel; clear or black versions
Limitations: A dot only marks a location and carries no meaning, so the user has to remember what each dot stands for. Adhesive bumps can come off with handling (general concern, not verified as a measured failure rate). They are not designed for the geometry of switch rockers.
Similarities to SPARSH: Removable, low-cost tactile marking added to existing controls with no rewiring. Used offline in everyday life.
Differences from SPARSH: Generic dots have no encoded meaning such as an appliance category, and no setup guidance. SPARSH caps are shaped to fit a switch, carry distinct shapes per appliance type, and come from an AI-assisted mapping of the board.

Product: 3M Bumpon Protective Products (e.g. SJ5302 Clear)
Target user: Industrial and general users: feet, stops and spacers. Not marketed for visually impaired users.
Main functionality: Self-adhesive hemispherical urethane bumper used as a foot, stop or spacer, which also reduces vibration and noise
Price: Not verified
Installation requirements: Peel and stick
Accessibility features: None by design; the raised dome can be felt
Limitations: Not designed for accessibility. The 3M page does not mention tactile or visually impaired marking. Same lack of encoded meaning as other bump dots.
Similarities to SPARSH: Cheap, removable, stick-on tactile cue
Differences from SPARSH: No semantic encoding and no fit to switch geometry

Product: Bump Dots (small/medium/large; black, clear, orange fluorescent; mixed packs)
Manufacturer: Sold by MaxiAids (USA); underlying manufacturer not verified
Target user: Blind and low-vision users
Main functionality: Adhesive tactile dots in several sizes, shapes and high-visibility colours, for marking appliance controls
Price: USD 2.60 to 2.75 per pack of about 20 to 25 dots. Mixed packs cost USD 4.95 (60 pieces), USD 6.95 (64 or 80 pieces) and USD 8.95. Source: https://www.maxiaids.com/category/tactile-markers
Installation requirements: Peel and stick
Accessibility features: Different shapes (round or square) and sizes give some tactile variety. Fluorescent orange gives high contrast for low-vision users.
Limitations: Only a few distinguishable shapes. No mapping to what a control does; the user or a helper has to remember it.
Similarities to SPARSH: Shape and size variation used as a tactile code. Cheap and removable.
Differences from SPARSH: Not designed for switch rockers and no guided setup. SPARSH uses a defined shape vocabulary for appliance categories plus a caregiver mapping step.

Product: Tactile marking pens and paints: HI MARK tactile pen (MaxiAids); Tactile Writing Liquid, Hi Marks replacement (LS&S); Raised 3D Marking Paint (Vision Australia)
Manufacturer: Retailers: MaxiAids, LS&S, Vision Australia. Original 'Hi-Marks' manufacturer not verified.
Target user: Blind and low-vision users and their helpers
Main functionality: Liquid squeezed from a tube that dries into raised, brightly coloured marks (dots, lines, circles) on plastic, metal, wood, cloth and paper
Price: LS&S Tactile Writing Liquid: USD 2.95 for a 1.25 oz tube (https://www.lssproducts.com/product/4121/211). MaxiAids HI MARK tactile pen: USD 3.95 (https://www.maxiaids.com/category/tactile-markers). Vision Australia Raised 3D Marking Paint: AUD 14.00 for 37 ml (https://shop.visionaustralia.org/raised-3d-marking-paint-black-37ml-bottle.html)
Installation requirements: Applied by hand. The LS&S page says it dries in about 2 hours depending on surface and thickness.
Accessibility features: Raised and high-contrast colours (orange, yellow, white, red, blue, black). Free-form shapes are possible.
Limitations: Semi-permanent: hard to remove cleanly from a switch and it can mark the plate (inferred from the product type, not verified). Marks drawn by hand are not uniform, and someone has to decide and remember what each mark means.
Similarities to SPARSH: Adds tactile cues to existing controls cheaply. Different shapes can encode meaning.
Differences from SPARSH: Not removable or reusable, and not standardised. SPARSH caps are removable, uniform, printed shapes with a defined vocabulary.

Product: RNIB PENfriend 3 audio labeller (DL128)
Manufacturer: RNIB (Royal National Institute of Blind People, UK)
Target user: Blind and partially sighted people
Main functionality: You record your own voice label onto a coded sticker. Touching the pen to the sticker plays the recording back. It also works as an MP3 and talking-book player.
Price: GBP 114.00 incl. VAT (GBP 95.00 excl. VAT; VAT relief available for eligible customers). Source: https://shop.rnib.org.uk/rnib-penfriend-3-93818
Installation requirements: Stick labels on items and record against them. Backups need a USB cable (not included) and Windows Label Manager software. Changing the SD card may need sighted help.
Accessibility features: Four tactile yellow buttons and audio instructions on the packaging
AI involvement: None (it plays recorded audio and does not recognise anything)
Limitations: The user has to carry the pen and point it at each label. It does not scan or read text. Label packs must be used in sequence, because duplicate numbers play the same recording.
Similarities to SPARSH: Personalised labels of controls that work offline. A helper can record labels at setup time.
Differences from SPARSH: Needs a powered device at every use and gives audio rather than touch feedback. Costs much more (GBP 114) than printed caps. Labels on small switch rockers could be hard to locate.

Product: 6dot Braille Label Maker
Manufacturer: 6dot (sold via Independent Living Aids and others)
Target user: Braille-literate blind users, teachers and organisations
Main functionality: Electronic braille embosser for label tape. You type on its built-in 6-key braille keyboard or a USB QWERTY keyboard, and it embosses, scores and cuts self-adhesive labels.
Price: USD 1,345.00 (Independent Living Aids listing). Source: https://independentliving.com/6dot-electronic-braille-label-maker/
Installation requirements: Stand-alone device; labels are stuck on by hand
Accessibility features: Braille keyboard, speaker and headphone alerts, all braille grades
Limitations: Only useful to braille readers. The price is high. A 3/8 in (9.5 mm) tape is wide relative to a 22.5 mm switch module and could cover the rocker (our inference).
Similarities to SPARSH: Tactile, offline labels fixed to existing objects
Differences from SPARSH: Needs braille literacy (SPARSH uses shapes) and costs far more

Product: Reizen RL-350 Braille Labeller
Manufacturer: Reizen (sold by See Differently / Royal Society for the Blind, Australia)
Target user: Braille readers and sighted helpers who don't know braille
Main functionality: Hand-held dial embosser. The dial shows braille on its upper rim and print letters on its lower rim; you line up a letter and squeeze to emboss it on tape.
Price: Not verified (not listed on the page)
Installation requirements: None; labels are stuck on by hand
Accessibility features: Print-and-braille dial, so a sighted caregiver can make braille labels
Limitations: Needs braille literacy to read the labels. A 12 mm tape is large for a switch rocker.
Similarities to SPARSH: A caregiver makes labels at setup time and the user reads them by touch offline
Differences from SPARSH: Uses text or braille rather than shape coding, and gives no help with mapping which switch controls which appliance

Product: Gira switch with touch symbols
Target user: Blind people and people with impaired eyesight
Main functionality: Recessed push-button or rocker light switch with large raised symbols for light, bell and door. An optional sound element confirms when the light is switched on.
Price: Not verified (not listed)
Installation requirements: Replaces the existing switch, so it needs an electrician and a compatible (European) wall box. Availability in India is not verified.
Accessibility features: Raised symbols per function, and audio confirmation that tells on from off
Limitations: You have to replace the hardware. It is designed for European systems, not Indian modular plates (inferred). It costs more than adding a marker (no price verified). Renters and short stays cannot replace switches.
Similarities to SPARSH: Uses shape and symbol coding of switch function for blind users, which is very close to SPARSH's tactile vocabulary
Differences from SPARSH: Permanent and installed by an electrician. SPARSH caps are removable retrofits for existing Indian modular switches with no rewiring.

Product: Wipro Smart Switch Retrofit Module (2 / 4 / 3+1 node; e.g. DSP2200, DSP2400)
Target user: General consumers who want to make existing switches smart
Main functionality: Module fitted behind existing switches so loads can be controlled by app or voice. Retailer listings say it is Alexa and Google Home compatible.
Price: MRP INR 2,690; sale INR 1,429 per unit (the official page showed it sold out). Source: https://wiproconsumerlighting.com/products/smart-product/smart-switch-module/wipro-smart-switch-retrofit-module-2-switch-control
Installation requirements: Wired behind the switchboard, which needs an electrician. Neutral wire requirement not verified on the official page.
Accessibility features: Voice control through Alexa or Google Assistant (from retailer listing titles, https://myelectric.in/?p=66957); app control
AI involvement: Indirect: cloud voice assistants do the speech recognition
Limitations: Needs Wi-Fi, a smartphone or smart speaker, and electrical work. Physical switches stay unlabelled. Whether the companion app works with screen readers is not verified.
Similarities to SPARSH: Solves 'which switch is which' for Indian switchboards without replacing the board
Differences from SPARSH: Uses voice or app instead of touch. Needs internet, power and wiring work. Costs much more per board.

Product: SONOFF MINI Extreme Wi-Fi Smart Switch (MINIR4)
Target user: DIY and home-automation users
Main functionality: Small Wi-Fi relay (ESP32) fitted behind an existing switch. Supports eWeLink app, Alexa and Google Assistant, timers, scenes and two-way control with the existing wall switch.
Price: GBP 11.76 (official UK store, https://sonoff.tech/en-uk/products/sonoff-mini-extreme-wi-fi-smart-switch-minir4). India retailer Electropi: INR 1,345 excl. 18% GST, out of stock when checked (https://www.electropi.in/sonoff-mini-r4-extreme-wi-fi-smart-switch)
Installation requirements: Wired into the wall box behind the switch, so it needs an electrician. Neutral wire likely required (SONOFF markets a separate no-neutral model) but not verified.
Accessibility features: Voice control through third-party assistants
Limitations: Same as the other smart retrofits: needs Wi-Fi, wiring and a smartphone. Not designed for accessibility.
Similarities to SPARSH: Retrofits existing switches rather than replacing the board
Differences from SPARSH: Electronic, needs electrical work and a network. Gives no tactile cue on the physical switch.

Product: Philips WiZ Smart Plug (16 A)
Target user: General consumers
Main functionality: Plug-in Wi-Fi socket adapter controlled through the WiZ app, Alexa or Google Assistant
Price: Sale INR 799 / INR 899 (variants); MRP INR 2,499. Source: https://in.shop.lighting.philips.com/products/philips-wiz-smart-plug
Installation requirements: Plugs into a socket; no wiring. Needs Wi-Fi and the app for setup.
Accessibility features: Voice control
Limitations: Only controls plug-in loads. Fans and lights on fixed switches cannot be controlled. Needs internet and setup.
Similarities to SPARSH: Cheap retrofit for India with no rewiring
Differences from SPARSH: Does not help identify the wall switches themselves

Product: Havells / Crabtree Signia Smart and Apogee Smart modular switches
Target user: General consumers and new builds
Main functionality: Replacement smart modules (relay switches, dimmers, fan regulators, scene controllers) with touch keys, app control (Havells DigiTap) and voice control
Price: Signia Smart 2 Channel Relay Switch 2M: INR 2,816. Signia Smart 4 Channel Relay 2M: INR 3,465. Apogee Smart 2 CH Relay: INR 6,188. Apogee Smart 1 CH Relay: INR 7,039 (special prices on the official page). Source: https://havells.com/green-energy/smart-home/smart-modular-switches.html
Installation requirements: Replaces modules in the existing board, so it needs an electrician. Apogee needs a mesh gateway (INR 4,641).
Accessibility features: Voice and app control
Limitations: Capacitive touch keys are flat and hard to find by touch (our inference). The MoHUA Harmonised Guidelines 2021, 4.15(14), ask that touch controls also have a tactile-button alternative. Cost and electrical work are also barriers.
Similarities to SPARSH: Targets the Indian modular switchboard
Differences from SPARSH: The trend toward flat touch panels makes switches less tactile. SPARSH adds tactile information to ordinary rocker switches.

Product: Roma Urban Smart Touch Series
Manufacturer: Panasonic Life Solutions India (formerly Anchor Electricals)
Target user: New and existing homes
Main functionality: Wi-Fi smart touch switches controlled by app, voice and a 'feather-touch' physical switch, with scenes and scheduling. Runs on a cloud platform managed by Panasonic India. Press release dated 23 Feb 2026.
Price: Not verified (not in the press release)
Installation requirements: Works with existing wiring and needs no gateway, per the release. Installation still means replacing switch modules (electrician).
Accessibility features: Voice and app control; which voice assistants are supported is not named
Limitations: Flat touch surface, cloud dependence and cost
Similarities to SPARSH: Indian modular ecosystem (Anchor Roma is a common board family)
Differences from SPARSH: Replaces hardware. Touch panels give fewer tactile cues than rockers.

Product: Amazon Alexa / Echo devices (VoiceView screen reader on Echo Show)
Target user: General consumers, including blind and low-vision users
Main functionality: Voice control of compatible smart switches and plugs, timers, information. Echo Show adds VoiceView (screen reader), a magnifier and colour correction or inversion.
Price: Not verified (varies by device)
Installation requirements: Needs Wi-Fi, the Alexa app for setup, and compatible smart switches or plugs to control lights and fans
Accessibility features: Voice-first interaction; VoiceView screen reader; magnifier
AI involvement: Yes: cloud speech recognition and natural-language understanding
Limitations: Only controls loads behind smart hardware. Needs internet. Does not help when a user meets an unfamiliar ordinary switchboard (hotel, relative's home, office). India: Amazon and NAB Uttar Pradesh deployed Echo-based learning in over 100 schools (Nov 2022), which shows the organisation already works with Alexa.
Similarities to SPARSH: Commonly used by blind people to control home devices
Differences from SPARSH: Needs a powered device, a network and smart hardware. SPARSH works on ordinary switches with no power or connection.

Product: Be My Eyes (with Be My AI)
Target user: Blind and low-vision people
Main functionality: Free video calls to sighted volunteers. Be My AI, described at launch as powered by GPT-4, takes a photo, gives a detailed description and answers follow-up questions in chat.
Price: Free for users (official site: 'Free and unlimited calls'). Source: https://www.bemyeyes.com/
Installation requirements: Smartphone app (iOS and Android) plus internet
Accessibility features: Designed for screen-reader users; human fallback
AI involvement: Yes: large multimodal model (GPT-4 per the 2023 announcement)
Limitations: Needs internet and a phone at every use. The user has to aim the camera. Be My Eyes itself warns about possible hallucinations and wrong answers (2023 beta announcement). Privacy concerns about sending images of the home.
Similarities to SPARSH: Could identify switch labels on demand. Used by visually impaired people to understand unfamiliar physical interfaces.
Differences from SPARSH: Help happens at the moment of use and depends on connectivity. SPARSH uses AI once at setup, then everyday use is offline and tactile.

Product: Seeing AI
Target user: Blind and low-vision people
Main functionality: Read (short text, documents, handwriting), Describe (scenes and photos, with Q&A), Products (barcodes), People, Currency, Find My Things, World (LiDAR spatial audio), Colors, Light (audible brightness tone)
Price: Free (App Store listing)
Installation requirements: Smartphone app
Accessibility features: Screen-reader-first design; audio guidance for document capture; the Light channel could detect whether a lamp is on
AI involvement: Yes: OCR, scene description, object recognition
Limitations: Needs a phone at every use. Cannot infer which switch controls which load unless the switch has a printed label. Aiming the camera is hard (VizLens reports 56.7% of blind participants' photos failed crowd quality checks, a related finding).
Similarities to SPARSH: AI camera assistance for visually impaired users
Differences from SPARSH: Help at the moment of use versus SPARSH's one-time setup and offline tactile use

Product: Lookout - Assisted vision
Target user: Blind and low-vision people
Main functionality: Modes: Text, Documents, Explore, Currency (including Indian Rupees), Food labels, Find (objects with direction and distance), Images (description and Q&A, English only)
Price: Not verified (the Play Store page shows an 'Install' button and no price; generally understood to be free)
Installation requirements: Android phone
Accessibility features: Available in more than 30 languages. The 2018 launch blog said core processing runs on the device and works without internet (whether that is still true is not verified).
AI involvement: Yes: on-device and cloud machine learning
Limitations: Needs a phone at every use. Image Q&A is English only. Cannot know the wiring mapping of a board.
Similarities to SPARSH: AI vision tool used in Indian contexts (supports INR currency)
Differences from SPARSH: Help at the moment of use, not a lasting tactile change

Product: Envision App and Envision Glasses
Target user: Blind and low-vision people
Main functionality: Text reading (60+ languages OCR), Describe Scene, Ask Envision (conversational AI over scans and images), colour detection, find objects and people, barcode scanning
Price: App: free (https://letsenvision.com/app). Glasses: USD 2,499 after a roughly 30% cut announced July 2023, possibly time-limited (https://www.letsenvision.com/blog/creating-a-more-accessible-envision). Current glasses price not verified.
Installation requirements: Smartphone, or the glasses; internet for most AI features (not verified per feature)
Accessibility features: Hands-free with the glasses
AI involvement: Yes: OCR and generative AI Q&A
Limitations: The glasses are expensive for Indian users. Needs a device at every use.
Similarities to SPARSH: AI to understand unfamiliar visual interfaces
Differences from SPARSH: Help at the moment of use and costs more

Product: Facade: Auto-generating Tactile Interfaces to Appliances (research prototype)
Manufacturer: Carnegie Mellon University and collaborators (Guo, Kim, Chen, Yeh, Hudson, Mankoff, Bigham), CHI 2017
Target user: Blind people using flat appliance control panels (e.g. microwaves)
Main functionality: The user photographs an appliance next to a dollar bill (for scale). Crowd workers label the buttons. The system generates a 3D-printable overlay of tactile buttons with 2-character braille abbreviations (or embossed letters or symbols). The user attaches it.
Price: The paper estimates under USD 10 per appliance from a printing service and under USD 5 for in-lab prints (Facade CHI 2017 paper)
Installation requirements: A 3D printer or printing service; the user attaches the overlay
Accessibility features: Braille abbreviations, different shapes for function buttons (rectangular) and number buttons (spherical), and a printable legend
AI involvement: Computer vision for perspective correction plus crowdsourcing (human labelling, not ML)
Limitations: Paper reports: only 34 of 55 photos (61.8%) warped successfully; 2 of 11 participants failed to attach the overlay; PLA was too rigid, so they moved to flexible NinjaFlex; braille errors came from print resolution; harder presses were needed; small interfaces may not fit braille.
Similarities to SPARSH: The closest prior work: photo-based mapping at setup, then a 3D-printed tactile retrofit used offline. Its lessons on materials (flexible versus rigid) and attachment apply directly.
Differences from SPARSH: Targets flat appliance membrane panels, not Indian modular rocker switchboards. Uses crowd workers instead of AI plus a caregiver. Uses braille instead of a shape vocabulary that works without braille literacy. Does not address 'which switch controls which load', which cannot be seen in a photo.

Product: VizLens: A Robust and Interactive Screen Reader for Interfaces in the Real World (research prototype)
Manufacturer: Carnegie Mellon University (Guo et al.), UIST 2016
Target user: Blind people using physical interfaces (microwaves, kiosks, thermostats)
Main functionality: Crowd workers label a reference photo. Afterwards, computer vision tracks the user's fingertip over the interface and speaks the button underneath.
Price: Crowd labelling averaged USD 1.15 per interface (paper)
Installation requirements: Smartphone plus a remote GPU server
Accessibility features: Real-time audio feedback and a guidance mode
AI involvement: Yes: computer vision (with human crowd labelling)
Limitations: Paper reports: 56.7% of blind participants' photos failed quality checks; interfaces with few visual features could not be recognised; the hand blocks the view; needs a remote GPU (about 200 ms latency).
Similarities to SPARSH: Labelling once at setup, then reusing the labels
Differences from SPARSH: Needs a phone and network at every use. A plain white Indian switchboard of identical rockers is the kind of low-feature interface VizLens struggled with (our inference from its stated limitation).
